Tango Mandarin
Citrus reticulata | UC Riverside Release | Mid–Late Season | Patent Expired 2025 — Royalty-Free
Whole fruit
Cross section
Late Jan – Apr
HARVEST WINDOW
22 – 222 lbs
YIELD PER TREE
<1 seed/fruit
SEED CONTENT
Fruit Characteristics
  • Size: 59 mm (2.32") diameter, 48 mm height
  • Weight: ~90 g (3.2 oz) per fruit
  • Shape: Deeply oblate, no neck
  • Rind color: Deep orange (RHS N25A) — very smooth
  • Flesh color: Deep orange-red, finely textured
  • Juice content: ~50% — abundant and juicy
  • Flavor: Rich, sweet, distinctive
  • Segments: 9–10 per fruit
  • Seeds: <1 per fruit (0.22 avg) even in mixed plantings
  • Peel: Easy to peel; thin rind (~3.0 mm)
  • Brix: 12.5% avg at maturity, ~14.4% by April
Harvest & Maturity
  • Matures late January in California's San Joaquin Valley
  • Peak harvest: February through March
  • Fruit holds quality on-tree through April
  • Storage: excellent at 5.6°C for up to 60 days
  • Production begins year 2 — one year ahead of most mandarins
Yield Performance
  • Year 2 trees: 10–26 kg (22–57 lbs) per tree
  • Year 3 trees: 33–58 kg (73–128 lbs) per tree
  • Mature tree range: 90–101 kg (198–222 lbs) in peak years
  • Alternate bearing: Low — less than other late mandarins
  • Planting density: 150–250 trees/acre
Estimated Yield — Per 1,000 Trees
Year 2 (light)~25 bins~$10,000
Year 3 (developing)~110 bins~$44,000
Mature, average~220 bins~$88,000
900 lbs/bin · $400/bin avg return · gross revenue only
Tree & Growing Notes
  • Developed at UC Riverside (released 2006) from irradiated W. Murcott budwood
  • Rootstock: Carrizo or C35 citrange — excellent compatibility
  • USDA Zones: 9–11; full sun, well-drained soil
  • Growth habit: Upright when young → spherical at maturity
  • Mature tree: ~3.7 m tall × 3.8 m wide
  • Sterile pollen: Won't seed neighboring blocks
Request a Quote →
Sources: Roose & Williams (2007). U.S. Plant Patent PP17863 — 'Tango' Mandarin. Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection, UC Riverside: citrusvariety.ucr.edu/crc4183 UCR News (Jan 2026): "Tango's sweet legacy lives on"
Shiranui Mandarin
Citrus reticulata hybrid | Ponkan × Kiyomi | Japanese Origin 1972 | Premium Specialty Market
Whole fruit
Cross section
Jan – Apr
HARVEST WINDOW
30 – 80 lbs
YIELD PER TREE
Variable
SEED CONTENT
Fruit Characteristics
  • Size: Large — 8–10 cm (3.1–3.9") diameter
  • Weight: ~280–340 g (10–12 oz) per fruit
  • Shape: Oblate with distinctive protruding "topknot"
  • Rind color: Deep orange-yellow, thick but loose-fitting
  • Flesh color: Deep orange, tender-crisp texture
  • Juice content: High — succulent and aqueous
  • Flavor: Exceptionally sweet (13–18° Brix)
  • Acidity: Below 1% citric acid
  • Seeds: Seedless when isolated; seedy if cross-pollinated
  • Peel: Very easy to peel — rind separates loosely from flesh
Harvest & Maturity
  • Matures January through April
  • Peak quality typically February through March
  • Limited commercial season — January through April only
  • Fruit develops sweetness in storage (post-harvest hold-out)
  • Cold-hardy to approximately 25°F
Yield Performance
  • Mature tree range: 30+ lbs per tree (14+ kg)
  • Premium pricing: Sumo Citrus® sells at $4–8/lb retail
  • Bearing age: 1–2 years after planting (precocious)
  • Production: Self-fertile, moderate productivity
  • Tree size: 4–8 ft mature — compact
Estimated Yield — Per 1,000 Trees
Year 3 (light)~12 bins~$10,800
Year 5 (developing)~45 bins~$40,500
Mature, average~80 bins~$72,000
900 lbs/bin · $400/bin avg return · gross revenue only
Tree & Growing Notes
  • Hybrid of Ponkan tangerine × Kiyomi tangor (Japan 1970s)
  • Officially released in Japan as Shiranui; also known as Dekopon
  • Imported to U.S. by Brad Stark Jr. in 1998, processed through CCPP at UCR
  • Rootstock: X-639, Carrizo, or C35 citrange
  • USDA Zones: 9–11 (frost-sensitive below 25°F)
  • Isolation required: Seeds develop if cross-pollinated by other citrus
  • Sumo Citrus® is a trademarked brand for Shiranui meeting specific quality standards
Request a Quote →
Sources: Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection, UC Riverside (CRC 4249): citrusvariety.ucr.edu/crc4249 Specialty Produce — Sumo Citrus® production records Karp, David. Los Angeles Times (2011). Shiranui import history

Reference Report — Tango Mandarin

Supporting Documentation for M&G Nursery Grower Claims
This document details the primary scientific and institutional sources used to support all yield, fruit quality, harvest window, and agronomic claims presented in the Tango Mandarin variety sheet. Each source is summarized with its key findings and the specific claims it supports.
1
U.S. Plant Patent PP17863 — Mandarin Tree Named 'Tango'
Authors
Mikeal L. Roose & Timothy E. Williams
Institution
University of California, Riverside — Dept. of Botany & Plant Sciences
Filed
September 2005; Published July 2007
Status
Expired September 6, 2025 — Royalty-free for U.S. growers
URL
patents.google.com/patent/USPP17863P3/en
YIELD FRUIT QUALITY SEED COUNT TREE CHARACTERISTICS
Yield per tree — 22 to 222 lbs (mature trees)
The patent reports fruit production on two-year-old trees averaging 10–26 kg (22–57 lbs) and three-year-old trees averaging 33–58 kg (73–128 lbs) across three California trial sites (Riverside, Santa Paula, Irvine). The original mother tree at Riverside yielded 98 kg (216 lbs) in year 5, 90 kg (198 lbs) in year 6, and 101 kg (222 lbs) in year 7.
Virtually seedless — <1 seed per fruit
The patent states Tango exhibits very low seed numbers — averaging just 0.22 seeds per fruit at Riverside under cross-pollination conditions, compared to 10–20 seeds/fruit for the parent W. Murcott. Tango's pollen has very low germination rates (<5%) and does not cause seeds in neighboring mandarins.
Production begins year 2; planting density 150–250 trees/acre
The patent specifies that fruit production begins in the second year after planting — one year earlier than most mandarin cultivars. Recommended planting densities range from 150–250 trees per acre using standard rootstocks including Carrizo and C35 citrange.
2
Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection — UC Riverside, Tango Entry

U.S. Plant Patent PP22096 — Mandarin Tree Named 'DaisySL'
Authors
Mikeal L. Roose & Timothy E. Williams
Institution
University of California, Riverside — Dept. of Botany & Plant Sciences
Filed
June 2009; Published 2010
URL
patents.google.com/patent/USPP22096P3/en
YIELD FRUIT QUALITY TREE CHARACTERISTICS CULTURAL PRACTICES
Yield per tree — 70 to 170 lbs (mature trees)
The patent reports fruit production on four-year-old trees averaging 27–48 kg (60–106 lbs) across four California trial sites. The original mother tree at Riverside yielded 77 kg (170 lbs) in year 7, demonstrating the alternate bearing pattern. This data forms the basis for the 70–170 lbs/tree range used in all yield estimates.
Near-seedless — ~2.2 seeds per fruit
The patent states DaisySL is very low seeded at 2.2 seeds/fruit in all cross-pollination situations, compared to 16–25 seeds/fruit for the original Daisy. In uniformly varietal commercial plantings, seed count is expected to be even lower.
Fruit characteristics — size, weight, juice, color, flavor
Patent data: fruit averages 68 mm (2.7") diameter and 60 mm (2.4") height. Average weight is 135 g (4.8 oz). Juice content averages 47%. Rind and flesh are very deep orange with smooth texture.
Full production begins year 3; planting density 150–250 trees/acre
Full fruit production begins in the third year after planting. Recommended planting densities range from 150–250 trees per acre using Carrizo and C35 citrange. Alternate bearing can be reduced through active fruit thinning.

Institution
UC Cooperative Extension, Ventura County

W. Murcott as the primary cultivar studied
YIELD PLANTING DENSITY PRODUCTION
Standard commercial planting: 14' × 18' = 170 trees/acre
UC's Ventura County cost study used W. Murcott as the model variety, with planting density of 170 trees per acre at 14' × 18' spacing. Variations of 100 to 300 trees per acre are documented depending on planting pattern (square, hedgerow, triangle).
Excellent production with little alternate bearing
W. Murcott is documented as having excellent production with minimal alternate bearing problems. By 2005, California had over 5,000 acres of W. Murcott planted, with cumulative plantings of 2–3 million trees by mid-2000s.
2
UCR Citrus Variety Collection — Self-Incompatibility & Pollination
Reference
Tracy Kahn, UCR Citrus Variety Collection
Publication
Topics in Subtropics Newsletter, UC ANR
POLLINATION ISOLATION REQUIREMENTS
Seedless only when isolated — seedy when cross-pollinated
W. Murcott is self-incompatible. Seedless to low-seeded fruit is produced only in isolated single-block plantings. When cross-pollinated by other citrus (mandarins, Valencias, Minneolas, lemons), fruit becomes seedy at 10–20 seeds per fruit — substantially reducing commercial value.
Strong pollinizer of Clementines
W. Murcott is a strong pollinizer for other mandarins, particularly Clementines. Adjacent Clementine plantings will develop seedy fruit. Growers must consider block layout carefully.

Mid-to-late maturing, exceptional storage on tree
Per UCR: Gold Nugget is a late-maturing diploid mandarin hybrid that combines good fruit size, excellent productivity, outstanding storage characteristics both on and off the tree, extremely rich and sweet fruit flavor, and the absence of seeds even in mixed plantings.

Gold Nugget has none to very few functioning pollen and ovules, producing seedless fruit regardless of neighboring citrus. This eliminates the isolation constraint that limits commercial Clementine and W. Murcott plantings.

C-35 has proven to be the best rootstock for Gold Nugget, moderating tree size, resisting root diseases, adapting well to different soils, and supporting the high-quality late-hanging fruit. Rich 16-6 trifoliate is also documented as suitable.

VARIETY ORIGIN PINK FLESH LYCOPENE
Pink flesh from lycopene — not a blood orange
Per UCR research, Cara Cara is not a blood orange. Blood oranges (Moro, Tarocco, Sanguinello) derive their purple-red flesh from anthocyanin pigments. Cara Cara's pink-salmon flesh comes from lycopene — the same red carotenoid antioxidant found in tomatoes. This distinction matters for both botanical accuracy and marketing positioning.
Spontaneous mutation from Washington navel
Cara Cara originated as a single bud sport observed on a Washington navel tree at Hacienda de Cara Cara in Venezuela in 1976. It has been propagated asexually since, maintaining the pink-flesh trait.

Arizona cultivar trials documented Cara Cara at 211 lbs per tree as a mid-season selection — greater than Zimmerman but in the intermediate range compared to Washington. Exterior fruit quality was rated intermediate, with more fancy grade and less juice grade than Beck or Fisher.

California heritage variety — Porterville origin 1895
Per Webber (1943): This variety originated about 1895 on the place of J.T. Bearss, a nurseryman at Porterville, California. All Persian limes carry wood pocket disease
Important commercial note from UCR: To date, all Persian lime trees are known to carry wood pocket, which can cause serious deterioration of the trees. This requires careful sanitary practices during propagation and field management. Budwood should be sourced from CCPP-certified material.

DEEPEST RED SPECIALTY MARKET FRUIT QUALITY
Released 1970 — first commercial deep-red grapefruit
Per Specialty Produce historical documentation: The Ruby Red grapefruit was the first grapefruit granted a United States patent (1929). In 1970, the now very popular Star Ruby variety was released, followed by the Rio Red variety in 1984. Star Ruby was the first commercially successful deep-red grapefruit, establishing the pigmented grapefruit market category.
Smaller than Rio Red, deeper color, slightly more seeds
Per Specialty Produce: Measuring about 3.25–4 inches in diameter, Star Ruby is smaller than the Ray Ruby and Rio Red varieties. Contains 1–6 seeds per fruit. The redder the flesh, the sweeter the taste. Standard pink grapefruit in taste, flavor and appearance — but with deepest color.

UCR Citrus Variety Collection — Chandler Pummelo
Maintainer
UC Riverside Citrus Research Center
Parent Cross
Siamese Sweet × Siamese Pink
Origin
Southern California — UCR program
UCR VARIETY LARGE FRUIT SWEET FLAVOR
UCR-developed Siamese cross with pink flesh
Per UCR documentation and Urban Harvest: Chandler is a hybrid of Siamese Sweet and Siamese Pink developed at UC Riverside. The red, fleshy slices are sweet and juicy with a flavor similar to grapefruit, but not so tart. The fragrant flowers and large fruit make it an outstanding ornamental as well as a productive edible.
Large fruit (2-4 lbs), few-to-no seeds
Per Stark Bro's commercial documentation and Urban Harvest: This huge, thick-skinned fruit can weigh up to 4 pounds. The skin is thick and tough but easy to peel. Light pink flesh with mild taste and slight bitter aftertaste. Few to no seeds — easily segmented. Cold-hardy to 22°F.

Available at UCR as part of specialty collection

Premium specialty market — "citrus caviar" for restaurants
Per industry trade documentation: Finger lime fruit splits open to reveal pearl-like vesicles in varying colors. These vesicles "pop" releasing intense lime flavor — earning the marketing name "citrus caviar" or "lime caviar." Premium pricing at $50-100+/lb is sustained by restaurant and cocktail program demand.

Reference Report — Buddha's Hand Citron

Supporting Documentation for M&G Nursery Grower Claims
This document details the primary scientific and institutional sources used to support all yield, fruit quality, harvest window, and agronomic claims presented in the Buddha's Hand Citron variety sheet. Each source is summarized with its key findings and the specific claims it supports.
1
UCR Citrus Variety Collection — Buddha's Hand Specialty Entry
Maintainer
UC Riverside Citrus Research Center
Scientific Name
Citrus medica var. sarcodactylis
Section
Specialty varieties collection
SPECIALTY CITRON LINEAGE ASIAN HERITAGE
Citron lineage — one of the 5 ancestral citrus species
Per UCR and Wikipedia: Buddha's hand is a mutation of Citron (Citrus medica), one of the five ancestral species of citrus fruits. Origin traces to South or East Asia, probably northeastern India or China. Different cultivars and variations form a gradient from "open-hand" types with outward-splayed segments to "closed-hand" types.
No juice, no pulp — peel and pith only
Per UF/IFAS Extension: Buddha's hand consists of thick, fleshy yellow peel that is the source of lemon fragrance. The peel is intensely fragrant — this is its primary commercial value. Used in perfumery, candied peel production, flavored liqueurs, and traditional Asian medicine.

Supporting Documentation for M&G Nursery Grower Claims

1
UCR Citrus Variety Collection — Kumquat Selections
Maintainer
UC Riverside Citrus Research Center
Genus
Fortunella — separate from main Citrus genus
Selections
Nagami (CRC 3877), Meiwa, Centennial variegated, Nordmann Seedless
MULTIPLE SELECTIONS EDIBLE PEEL COLD HARDY
Nagami vs Meiwa — distinct flavor profiles
Per US Citrus Nursery documentation: Meiwa kumquats offer sweetness throughout — both peel and flesh are sweet, creating a consistent, pleasant eating experience. Nagami kumquats present a sweet-tart contrast — sweet peel with distinctly sour flesh, creating a more complex experience. Meiwa fruits are shorter and more oblong-round; Nagami are more elongated and oval.
Eaten whole — peel and all
Per UCR documentation: Kumquats are unique among citrus in that the fruit is consumed whole — peel and flesh together. The peel is sweet on both Nagami and Meiwa varieties. This eating pattern, combined with small fruit size and cold-hardiness, makes kumquats excellent specialty/ornamental citrus.

Rootstock Reference Guide
Comparison of M&G Nursery's six rootstock offerings
Choosing the right rootstock is one of the most consequential decisions in citrus production. Rootstock affects mature tree size, fruit quality, disease tolerance, soil compatibility, salt tolerance, and cold hardiness — all of which compound over the 30+ year life of an orchard.

M&G Nursery offers six rootstocks covering the full range of California growing conditions, from premium high-density plantings to challenging marginal soils. Each rootstock is described below with its specific strengths, ideal use cases, and limitations.
Carrizo Citrange
Citrus sinensis × Poncirus trifoliata
The most widely-used commercial rootstock in California. Balanced performance, good disease tolerance, moderate vigor.
Characteristics
Tristeza (CTV)Tolerant — primary reason for industry adoption
Cold-hardinessHardy — withstands ~20°F
Soil pH preference5.5–7.5 — moderate acidic to neutral
Salt toleranceLow — avoid saline irrigation
Calcareous soilsPoor performance on high-lime soils
Heavy clayAcceptable — better than C35
VigorModerate
Tree size inducedStandard
Fruit qualityExcellent — high juice content, good sugar/acid ratio
PhytophthoraTolerant
NematodesModerately tolerant
Best for
  • Tango, DaisySL, Cara Cara, Fukumoto navels
  • Most mandarins requiring moderate vigor
  • Tristeza-prone areas (most of California)
  • Heavy clay soil sites
Limitations
  • Avoid in highly calcareous or saline soils
  • Lower drought tolerance than Macrophylla
  • Not ideal for very alkaline sites
C35 Citrange
Citrus sinensis × Poncirus trifoliata
Tree-size moderating rootstock. Smaller mature canopy enables higher-density plantings and easier picking.
Characteristics
Tristeza (CTV)Tolerant
Cold-hardinessHardy — comparable to Carrizo
Soil pH preference5.5–7.0 — best on acid to neutral soils
Salt toleranceLow — sensitive to chloride
Calcareous soilsPoor performance
Heavy clayLess tolerant than Carrizo
VigorModerate to low — size-controlling
Tree size induced~80% of standard — high-density compatible
Fruit qualityExcellent — superior to Carrizo for some varieties
PhytophthoraTolerant
NematodesModerately tolerant
Best for
  • Gold Nugget mandarin (preferred rootstock)
  • High-density mandarin plantings
  • Sites where smaller tree canopy is preferred
  • Premium varieties where fruit quality matters most
Limitations
  • Heavy clay soils — Carrizo is better
  • Calcareous/alkaline soils — use trifoliate alternatives
  • Salt-affected sites — use Macrophylla instead
Rich 16-6 Trifoliate
Poncirus trifoliata
Pure trifoliate orange. Maximum cold hardiness, dwarfing tree size, exceptional fruit quality, but soil-restrictive.
Characteristics
Tristeza (CTV)Tolerant
Cold-hardinessHighest among rootstocks

Salt toleranceLow
Calcareous soilsPoor — avoid high-lime soils entirely
Heavy clayTolerant
VigorLow — dwarfing rootstock
Tree size induced~60-70% of standard — dwarfing
Fruit qualityOutstanding — highest sugar/acid ratios
PhytophthoraTolerant
NematodesTolerant
Best for
